intro: Lena Kowalski works in a hospital’s reporting team. She is good with spreadsheets and has never built a database. When the hospital starts a data modernisation project, she volunteers, and then immediately wonders what she has signed up for. DP-900 is her way in.
Follow Lena as she learns where data lives, how it is stored, and how it becomes a dashboard someone trusts.

core-data-concepts: Lena’s first week: the admissions system adds a patient record every few seconds, while finance runs a heavy report once a month over a whole year of billing. Two very different jobs, and she learns the names for them: many small transactions versus a few big analyses. She also meets the idea that data comes in tidy tables, loose documents, and files like images and scans, and that each needs different handling.
relational-data-on-azure: The hospital’s existing system uses tables, keys that link patients to appointments, and a lot of overnight jobs. Lena learns why tables are split up to avoid repeating data, and how Azure offers several ways to host a SQL database. The team wants to move with as little rewriting as possible, so she learns which option keeps the old jobs working and which is a better fit for new apps.
non-relational-data-on-azure: A research group wants to track which staff collaborate on which projects, including collaborators of collaborators. Lena finds that this kind of relationship question is awkward for tables and much easier in a graph. She tours the other storage options: documents, key-value tables, blobs for scans, files for shared folders, and a data lake for everything that arrives raw.
data-warehousing-and-pipelines: Finance wants sales by region by quarter for the last five years. Lena learns that this means a warehouse built around facts and dimensions, filled by a pipeline. She compares transforming data before loading it with loading it raw and transforming afterwards, and finds out when each is sensible. She also sees why some data is processed overnight in batches and some as it arrives.
modern-analytics-platforms-and-bi: The final piece is the executive dashboard. It needs to be live, but the underlying queries are occasional and unpredictable. Lena looks at the Azure services for analytics, streaming and a unified platform, and at the choice between importing data into a report or querying it live. She finally sees how every earlier chapter ends up on one screen.

epilogue: On the morning of the exam Lena opens the hospital dashboard one last time. It is live, trusted and fed by the pipeline she now understands from end to end. The exam questions use unfamiliar names for familiar ideas, and Lena is surprised at how many of them she can picture.

core-data-concepts: Lena tries to run the year-end billing report directly on the admissions system, in the middle of the morning rush. The system, which was built for many tiny transactions, groans and slows down. A nurse in the ward asks why a patient record takes thirty seconds to open. Lena learns that the two kinds of work are best kept in separate places.
relational-data-on-azure: Lena stores a patient’s address in every appointment row ‘to save joins’. When a patient moves, the address is wrong in forty places and right in two. A good table design would have kept it in one. Lena now believes in keys with the zeal of the newly converted.
non-relational-data-on-azure: Lena models the research collaborations as documents, each listing the colleagues. A simple question, ‘who knows someone who knows Dr. Patel?’, now needs a series of lookups, like asking a family tree for directions. A graph database, she realises, was built for exactly this question.
data-warehousing-and-pipelines: Lena sets up a nightly pipeline that loads the raw data straight into the finance report. The report now includes duplicates, test entries and one patient called ‘Test Patient’. The board are intrigued by Test Patient’s spending habits. Transforming and cleaning before reporting is, it turns out, the point of a pipeline.
modern-analytics-platforms-and-bi: Lena builds the executive dashboard in import mode and says it is ‘live’. It was last refreshed on Tuesday. The CEO checks Thursday’s sales and is, politely, confused. Live queries, a different mode, would have shown the truth, albeit a little more slowly.

core-data-concepts.problem: Different kinds of data and workload are mixed together and perform badly.
core-data-concepts.cause: Data comes in tables, documents and files, and workloads are either many small updates or large analyses.
core-data-concepts.solution: The chapter names data types, transactional versus analytical work, the ACID guarantees and the roles that handle each.
core-data-concepts.next: Next, how relational data is organised and hosted in Azure.

relational-data-on-azure.problem: Data repeated in many places goes out of date and wastes space.
relational-data-on-azure.cause: Tables without keys or normalisation duplicate facts, and hosting choices are picked without knowing what each supports.
relational-data-on-azure.solution: Keys, normalisation and indexes organise data well, and Azure’s SQL options match different migration and management needs.
relational-data-on-azure.next: Next, data that does not fit neat tables.

non-relational-data-on-azure.problem: Some data, such as relationships, documents and raw files, does not fit rows and columns.
non-relational-data-on-azure.cause: A single storage model is forced onto all kinds of data.
non-relational-data-on-azure.solution: Cosmos DB and its APIs, table, blob, file and lake storage give a fitting home to each type.
non-relational-data-on-azure.next: Next, bringing data together for analysis.

data-warehousing-and-pipelines.problem: Raw data from many sources is hard to analyse and report on.
data-warehousing-and-pipelines.cause: Data arrives in different shapes, at different times, with errors.
data-warehousing-and-pipelines.solution: Star schemas, ETL and ELT, batch and streaming, and Data Factory organise and move it into a form ready for analysis.
data-warehousing-and-pipelines.next: Next, the platforms and tools that turn it into reports.

modern-analytics-platforms-and-bi.problem: Reports are stale, slow or hard to share.
modern-analytics-platforms-and-bi.cause: Analysis tools are chosen without knowing how each handles scale, cost and freshness.
modern-analytics-platforms-and-bi.solution: Synapse, Databricks, Stream Analytics, Fabric and Power BI cover different needs, and report modes balance freshness and speed.
modern-analytics-platforms-and-bi.next: That completes the lessons. Next come the cheat sheet, the word bank and the practice questions.
